title: Buffer API: Access, Rate Limits, Errors (2026 Guide)
summary: Buffer API credentials must be created in your account and sent with every request. Your subscription plan determines rate limits and error handling.
body_markdown:
## The strongest case against building on Buffer's API


Don't depend on a layer that sits between you and the networks, says the objection. Buffer is a scheduling product with a narrow API, gated access and a record of changing what it offers, so going direct or using a unified social API buys control.


A cap you can't confirm can break your feature.


### Limited Buffer API surface and access restrictions


If your feature needs a network-specific option that Buffer hasn't exposed, you wait or you drop it. The API exists to serve Buffer's product: queues, scheduled posts, connected channels. Anything the scheduler doesn't model is out of reach.


A closed catalogue only grows where its vendor chooses to spend, so a missing connector means waiting on someone else's priorities.[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/) lets you generate the missing integration with AI and add it privately to your own instance, with no vendor release in between.


**Roughly 60% of its 750 integrations were contributed** by the community, a count you can reproduce from the open-source monorepo on GitHub, meaning you don't have to trust Buffer's representation of community contribution.


On top of that, access is granted, not assumed. If Buffer decides who may build on the API, your project depends on that decision going your way, and going your way again whenever the terms are reviewed.


### Buffer API dependence on one vendor's roadmap


Here is the sharpest point of the objection: **Buffer has changed API availability before** . Your integration then inherits a decision made for Buffer's own priorities.


Say it plainly, as the proponents of going direct do: you are building a second-order dependency, on Buffer, which depends on each network. A change at either level reaches your users, and you have no vote at the first.


### Cost of using network APIs instead of Buffer


Its supporters should say so: going direct isn't free of constraint. Each network brings its own app review, its own authentication flow, its own limits and its own habit of changing them. You would maintain one integration per network, and each one can break independently.


To compress that work into a single contract, you can use a unified social API, but then the dependency is a different vendor, with its own pricing and roadmap.


Either way you pay: direct access gives you control over the call and the failure, at the price of owning every integration. Buffer gives you one integration and takes the control.
